financial_summary: Alamos Gold Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $13.3B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +30% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +9.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $288M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.90× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 0.3%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 4.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 61% operating margin runs 51pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.63x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+24.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 43% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 56% and a beta of 0.80, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.55 vs 5y 0.68), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $105.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 28% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $11.99 (margin of safety -166%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 39%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $9.38 to $15.84 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Basic Materials peers: cheaper on P/E 12.6 vs 16.5, richer on P/FCF 46.2 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 30% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 2.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $40.67 on average, 28% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.17).
It converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 20% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 36pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $423.1M.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 30.1% over 3 years and 19.3% over 5 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
Free cash flow has compounded 18.7% a year over five years.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 4.3% on average.
Analysts expect 28.5% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 75%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.3% (0.5% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 16 consecutive years, raising it 87.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,400 employees, each generates about $754K of revenue, 1.2x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 15.7% a year.
That works out to $120K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
